title: Soviet Nostalgia Is a Geopolitical Dead End
gist: Ani Chkhikvadze argues that Western 'realists' urging Ukraine to accept Moscow's demands (Carlson, Mearsheimer, Sachs, Chomsky et al.) are driven by Soviet-era fatalism: they diagnose Ukraine's weaknesses correctly but prescribe the wrong cure, since concessions to Putin are only a down payment. She contends Ukraine wins if it stays sovereign and Western-aligned, urges more air defense and pressure on Russia, and notes there is not yet a Western consensus to do so.

insights.claim: Chkhikvadze says left and right commentators—Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens, Marjorie Taylor Greene, John Mearsheimer, Noam Chomsky, Jeffrey Sachs, Owen Matthews—converge on the belief that Kyiv must eventually accept Moscow's demands.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Influential Western voices pushing settlement shape political pressure on Ukraine aid.
insights.quote: Sooner or later, Kyiv must learn to live with Moscow’s demands.
insights.locator: The left and the right rarely agree

insights.claim: The author concedes the pessimists' diagnosis—Ukraine is short of men, money and Patriot interceptors, corruption persists, and allies' declarations outrun their policies—but says their cure is wrong.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Air-defense interceptor shortages are a binding constraint; demand for Patriot-class systems stays high.
insights.quote: They are right about the diagnosis and wrong about the cure.
insights.locator: What is striking is how many people

insights.claim: Realist forecasters predicted Ukraine would lose in 2022 and every year since, and rather than revising their premise they keep moving the date forward.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Treat perennial 'Ukraine collapse imminent' forecasts skeptically.
insights.locator: The worst part of this so-called realist

insights.claim: The author frames this 'realism' as an old Russian fatalism in which Russian power is constant, Western resolve fickle and Ukrainian resistance doomed—akin to the Brezhnev Doctrine.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: A lens for discounting deterministic narratives about Russian inevitability.
insights.quote: It calls itself realism, but it is really pessimism, in which history can change everything except Russia’s behavior.

insights.claim: Motives for the recurring argument include hatred of the West, audience economics (outrage and fringe takes sell), sympathy for Russia's strongman, and fear.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Media incentives sustain pro-settlement narratives regardless of battlefield facts.
insights.locator: Why, then, does the argument keep returning?

insights.claim: Russia's advances have come at enormous cost and been so slow that 'a snail set off from its starting positions might have reached parts of today’s front line first.'
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Slow attritional front argues against imminent Russian breakthrough scenarios.
insights.quote: a snail set off from its starting positions might have reached parts of today’s front line first

insights.claim: Ukraine need not recover all its territory to win: if it remains sovereign, secure and in the West, Russia's larger project will have failed.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Redefines 'success' around sovereignty and Western integration—relevant to reconstruction and EU accession plays.
insights.quote: It need not recover all its territory to win.

insights.claim: Even serious skeptics concede Putin has not changed his war aims and that Jared Kushner is naive to think business deals will seduce the Kremlin into peace.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Business-deal-driven peace efforts with Russia are unlikely to deliver durable settlements.
insights.locator: Even the more serious skeptics concede

insights.claim: Concessions to a maximalist Putin are only a down payment, as Georgia's 2008 cease-fire and the Minsk agreements were followed by further Russian invasions.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Ceasefire deals carry high re-escalation risk; don't price a ceasefire as durable peace.
insights.quote: A concession to a man who demands the maximum will only be a down payment.
insights.locator: Even the more serious skeptics concede

insights.claim: Moscow used force in Moldova and Georgia in the early 1990s before NATO enlargement was an available excuse, undercutting the claim that NATO provoked the war.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Undermines the NATO-provocation thesis used to argue for concessions.
insights.quote: The only power that has invaded anyone in the neighborhood is Russia.

insights.claim: The Baltic states joined NATO despite warnings Russia would never tolerate it, because Western governments decided policy should move while Russia was weak.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Western policy choices, not Russian vetoes, have historically set outcomes.
insights.locator: Soviet power once looked equally permanent

insights.claim: The author argues the West should supply more air defense and increase pressure on Russia until the war ends as a strategic loss for Moscow, even if Russia takes the rest of the Donbas, and should guarantee Ukraine's future security.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Advocacy for sustained air-defense and security guarantees supports defense-industrial demand.
insights.quote: If Ukraine lacks air defense, the answer is more air defense.

insights.claim: There is not yet a Western consensus on guaranteeing Ukraine's security and pressuring Russia, which the author warns will bring problems closer to home.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Lack of consensus keeps Ukraine policy volatile and European security risk elevated.
insights.quote: Is there a Western consensus on this yet? No.

insights.claim: Young Ukrainians speak more Ukrainian, consume less Russian culture and understand fewer Soviet references, eroding the shared post-Soviet cultural space.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Durable cultural decoupling from Russia supports Ukraine's long-run Western orientation.
insights.quote: Young Ukrainians speak more Ukrainian, consume less Russian culture

insights.claim: After nearly five years of war the author finds it hard to imagine Ukrainians choosing capitulation, and predicts the Russian empire will eventually collapse, including in people's heads.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Ukrainian resolve makes a capitulation-based settlement unlikely.
